quote: Religion… shall mean for us the feelings, acts, and experiences of individual men in their solitude; so far as they apprehend themselves to stand in relation to whatever they may consider the divine.
content: James’s full sentence begins “Religion, therefore, as I now ask you arbitrarily to take it, shall mean for us…” (Varieties, Lecture II). It is a stipulation for the scope of a lecture series, announced as arbitrary, and James explains in the same passage that he is setting institutional religion aside not because it is inferior but because the personal experience is the part a psychologist can study, the institutions being “second-hand.” The essay reads this as a doctrine that sacredness must be private and as evidence that James “admired” solitude as loneliness. James’s book is a naturalistic psychology of religious experience, written by the founder of American psychology, treating conversion, mysticism and saintliness as phenomena with causes and “fruits” to be judged by their effects; it is, that is, the program the essay Dissolving the Question recommends, applied to religion in 1902. The essay finds Dark Side Epistemology in the framing of the one classic that did what the essay says should be done, on the strength of a sentence quoted without its first clause.

quote: Faith—in the early days of religion, when people were more naive, when even intelligent folk actually believed that stuff, religions staked their reputation upon the testimony of miracles in their scriptures. And Christian archaeologists set forth truly expecting to find the ruins of Noah’s Ark. But when no such evidence was forthcoming, then religion executed what William Bartley called the retreat to commitment
content: The chronology runs backwards. Faith as commitment independent of evidence is as old as Christian theology: Tertullian’s credibile est, quia ineptum est (c. 200), Augustine’s and Anselm’s credo ut intelligam, Luther’s hostility to reason in matters of faith, and Kierkegaard’s leap (1840s) all precede the Ark expeditions, which are a twentieth-century phenomenon (the Navarra and Ararat searches begin in the 1950s). Bartley’s The Retreat to Commitment (1962) is about Protestant theology’s response to the Enlightenment critique, Barth and Tillich, not to archaeology. The essay’s story, that religion first bet on evidence, lost, and then retreated, is the Whig history of religion that Book II’s annotations found in Fake Beliefs: a sequence invented to fit the thesis that faith is a defensive adaptation to disconfirmation. The historical relation is closer to the reverse; the evidentialist apologetics (Paley, the nineteenth-century harmonists) is the late arrival, a response to the Enlightenment, and the fideist strand is original. Nothing in the essay’s argument needs the false sequence, which is a reason to wonder why it was told.

quote: Religion is a poisoned chalice, from which we had best not even sip. Spirituality is the same cup after the original pellet of poison has been taken out, and only the dissolved portion remains—a little less directly lethal, but still not good for you.
content: The line about spirituality has an unexpected empirical friend, and the line about religion does not. In a large British community sample, people who described themselves as spiritual but not religious had higher rates of anxiety, phobia, drug dependence and abnormal eating attitudes than either the religious or the neither (King et al. (2013)), a pattern found in other samples since; whatever spirituality-without-religion is, it does not carry the protective correlations that religion does. Those protective correlations, on the best evidence, run through the congregation rather than the creed (Lim & Putnam (2010), discussed in Book II): the well-being gain of the religious is explained by friendships made at services. The essay’s own remedy, the sacred “shared in togetherness with the many other onlookers,” is the social component, and it is the component institutional religion is best at and private spirituality worst at. So the data agree with the essay about spirituality and disagree with its diagnosis of religion, in which the corruption is privacy; the privacy is what the religious have least of, and what the essay is proposing to keep.
